name: Salmon Pink
lede: Salmon pink borrows the flesh of the fish for a warm pink, and the name has been used for a range of colors from rosy pink to orange-red.

sections.title: Which salmon pink
sections.body: The screen swatch here is a clear, light pink [1]. Older uses are often more orange: the library's earliest source is the German RAL list of 1927, whose matching swatch is a duller coral-orange, and the xkcd survey of 2010 gives yet another [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files our swatch under strong pink, about four units away, and the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 is among the sources [1]. In short, the name points at a family of salmon-flesh colors, not one fixed hue. For neighbors see [[salmon]], [[light-salmon]] and [[coral]].

sections.title: In print and in cloth
sections.body:
The Financial Times has been printed on salmon-pink newsprint since January 1893 [2]. In 1990 the paper failed in an attempt to stop the Evening Standard from running its business pages in a similar shade, a case Paterson uses to show how hard it is to protect a color [2]. Paterson also notes that the pink of farmed salmon is produced by feeding the fish a dye, astaxanthin [3].

On the dye side, Finlay describes two weavers in the Oaxaca highlands who found salmon-pink in rock lichens, deep browns in walnuts and the gold of pomegranate [4]. Gage points out how Van Gogh, copying a Hiroshige print, pushed its soft greens and salmon-pinks into bright complementary greens and reds [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Only one painting in our archive of 23,781 holds this swatch over a meaningful share of the canvas, as photographed [1]. In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1930s and rose fastest in the 1910s, by Google Books [1]. Photographs of aged, varnished paintings show how a picture looks now, not what the painter mixed [1].
